newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's PAP sweeps back to power before vote.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's PAP sweeps back to power before vote.

text.p: The ruling People's Action Party (PAP), which has run Singapore since 1959, swept back to power on Monday before a single vote was cast.
"We are already in government," Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong told reporters shortly after nominations closed. The government said PAP had won 47 uncontested seats in the 83-member parliament.
The Election Commission said later that voting would take place on January 2, giving the minimum nine day campaign allowed following the close of nominations.

The opposition parties held only four seats in the old 81-member parliament and said they would adopt a by-election strategy for the general elections, picking races in which they might have a chance.
They will contest six of the 15 multi-member group representation constituencies (GRCs), where votes are cast as slates, and all nine single seat wards.
Both the PAP and the main opposition Workers Party (WP), which is putting up 14 candidates, are campaigning on giving back some power to the people.
The PAP plans to do this by devolving some functions, especially in education, social services and the improvement of housing estates, to local communities and their members of parliament.
Goh, who was returned unopposed, said this was why voters should elect the best candidates as they will form the "local government".
The WP, motto "Power to the People", hopes the voters turn Singapore into a "real democracy", party leader J.B. Jeyaretnam told a news conference.
The PAP has launched a tough campaign to keep the opposition out of parliament.
Ministers toured constituencies over the weekend with a stark message -- vote for the opposition and forget any prospect of getting lavish government renovation and development schemes.
Goh was the bluntest, telling people on Sunday he would respect their choice if they voted for the opposition.

But, he added: "Then you'll be left behind, then in 20,30 years' time, the whole of Singapore will be bustling away and your estate, through your own choice, will be left behind. They become slums. That's my message."
Singapore has blossomed under the PAP into a thriving, modern city where the per capital gross domestic product is higher than in Britain, the former colonial power.
The PAP is sometimes criticised abroad for its patriarchal government of a city-state where murderers and drug traffickers are hanged and lesser offenders caned.
But Goh shrugs off such perceptions. He told students on Friday that Singapore could not have become what it has if the opposition had been given a chance.
"Do you think we could have done even half of what was achieved in the last 30 years if we had a multi-party system and a revolving door government?" he asked.
"Do you think we could have done just as well if we had a government which was constantly being held in check by 10 to 20 opposition members in the last 30 years?"

Political analysts said the most keenly watched aspect of the elections will be the percentage of the PAP vote, and whether its running one-third new candidates will reverse a decline to 59.3 percent in 1991 from 75.6 percent in 1980.
Analysts say a PAP victory ahead of elections might encourage the vote for the opposition, as happened in 1991.

"It is a generally accepted fact that a large part of the opposition's support stems from Singaporeans' desire to have opposition voices in parliament and not so much from their wanting an alternative government," Straits Times columnist Chua Lee Hoong wrote on Sunday.
